title: Tomorrow Is Still Ours to Shape
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Writing on Election Day, Kathleen Schafer invites leaders to pause and notice whether they feel fearful, hopeful, or exhausted before the flood of predictions and results arrives. She argues that Conscious Choice may be the most important leadership skill to develop, and that it begins with distinguishing between having an opinion about what is happening and being intentional about what we want to create. Opinions come from experience, values, and beliefs, while intentions guide how those values show up in choices and action. That capacity grows as leaders know themselves more deeply, understand what matters most, and see how thoughts and emotions shape their decisions. She states the kind of community she wants to help build, one where people can disagree profoundly and still recognize shared humanity, and she closes with three reflection questions and a Grace Lee Boggs line about doing something local and real.
points: We cannot always choose our first feelings, but we can choose what we do with them, and that is the space where leadership operates.
Conscious Choice separates opinion about circumstances from intention about what we want to create.
Self-knowledge, including values, gifts, and awareness of how emotions steer decisions, widens the room to respond rather than react.
Responsibility for the communities we build continues well beyond the event that dominates the news cycle.
The closing reflection questions turn the essay into a short personal exercise on what to carry forward and what to contribute.
quotes: We may not always be able to choose our initial feelings, but we have considerable capacity to decide what we do with them. We can become consumed by reacting to circumstances, or we can remain connected to ourselves and consider how best to contribute.
Conscious Choice begins with understanding the difference between having an opinion about what is happening and being intentional about what we want to create.
Our opinions are informed by our experiences, values, and beliefs. Our intentions guide how we bring those values into the world through our choices and actions.

When we understand what matters most to us, recognize the unique gifts we bring, and become aware of how our thoughts and emotions influence our choices, we create space to respond with intention, even when circumstances are difficult or the way forward is unclear.

I want us to be able to disagree, even profoundly, while continuing to recognize our shared humanity. And I want more of us to experience the joy that comes from using our gifts to contribute to something larger than ourselves.
Elections shape the conditions in which we live, and those conditions deserve our full attention. Our responsibility for the lives and communities we are creating continues well beyond Election Day.
